content_metadata.description: This video delves into the vision and groundbreaking technology proposed by Ben Glass for airborne wind turbines. It explores the potential of high-altitude wind power to address global challenges in infrastructure and clean energy.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: People start working on the really important problems.
The problems that have real global impact, real human impact.
I think getting more of the smartest people in the world to focus on solving these kind of big
global challenges as opposed to making the next Instagram, the next Twitter.
One very interesting area for me personally is kind of the nexus of energy and water and food and
health. I think a lot of these are very interconnected and it's just an area that I personally think
is really interesting. There's a lot of exciting opportunities there. I've got a lot of visions right
right now. We're looking at really revolutionizing infrastructure for all the developing
world markets, rural areas, places that don't have the infrastructure that we kind of take for
granted here in Germany or in the US both in terms of access to energy, access to cheap energy,
ideally clean energy, access to communication networks, access to the internet. We're trying to
make it a lot less expensive and a lot quicker to build out the infrastructure in those places.
The idea behind the airborne wind turbine that we're developing is to take
leverage all of the work over the last few decades that has gone to make wind turbines the
very efficient, very mature technology they are. We take that and we combine it with this
aerostat technology. We're taking two proven technologies bringing them together which opens
up a whole new possibility by in order to harness the winds above what you can reach with a tower.
The reason that we're interested in high-altitude winds is because as you move up off the ground,
winds actually become much faster and much, much more powerful. You kind of get a sense of this if
you go and fly a kite, you know that the higher you get it up there the stronger the winds, the
the easier it is to keep aloft. That's also the same reason that wind turbines are getting bigger
and bigger today and they're putting them on taller and taller towers. It's to try to reach those
strong, consistent winds. So we decided let's get rid of the tower, let's get rid of that foundation,
let's kind of skip this incremental increase in height and just go all the way up there.
We've basically developed a tethered autonomous airborne platform. So think of the blimps or the
zeppelins that you see flying above sports games. We take that same basic technology. We use kind
of the industrial cousin of the blimps you're used to seeing, they're called aerostats. The aerostats
are essentially tethered balloons or tethered blimps. They've been used for really for decades
in a military setting to lift radar and other kind of surveillance and communications equipment.
So what we've done is we've taken that basic technology and we've actually created an auto pilot
or we've automated all the operations. So these systems can launch, they can land, they can fly
without having to have any people there, anyone kind of in the loop controlling it. There's certainly
a lot of automation which is a form of artificial intelligence and that automation allows the system
to kind of take all of the inputs from all of the sensors on board. It allows it to
communicate to some of the local and regional weather stations and it runs through a number of
algorithms to decide how to operate whether it should launch, whether it should land, you know,
where to fly, what altitude to fly at. We generate electricity aloft just like any other wind turbine.
We actually send that electricity that power down to the ground via one of our tethers that has
a conductive cable embedded into the tether and you know at the end of the day we're just another
generator. We're making systems that aren't really consumer facing. They're pretty big industrial
equipment so we're very much a B to B business and our customers tend to be you know large utilities
are industrial corporations. In 10 years you know we'll hopefully have been wildly successful at
deploying flying wind turbines all over the world and helping to build out the communication
infrastructure that'll bring the three billion people that don't have access to the internet
online and I think that you know my vision for Alterus is that this is just the start and that we
continue to drive for innovative solutions to really to whatever the most pressing problems in 10
years are.

youtube_description:
We all know wind turbines bound to the ground. But the higher you go up in the air, the stronger the winds get. So why not forget the tower and place the turbine on tethered blimps at high altitude? Ben Glass, founder and CEO of Altaeros Energies, Somerville MA (USA), has the vision to generate clean energy for rural areas with little infrastructure. How exactly does it work and what's the business idea behind it?

Windräder kennt man, aber eigentlich müssten sie hoch oben in der Luft schweben, denn dort sind die Winde viel stärker. Warum setzt man sie also nicht auf eine Art Zeppelin? Ben Glass, Gründer und Geschäftsführer von Altaeros Energies aus den USA erzählt seine Vision, wie man günstig saubere Energie für Gegenden produzieren könnte, in denen es an Infrastruktur mangelt. Wie genau soll das funktionieren und wie wird daraus ein Geschäft?

Das Interview entstand am Rande des Zukunftskonkgresses 2016 des 2bAHEAD ThinkTanks.
